# The goal
You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 12 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.

- You have exactly 4096 tokens to think. If you reach 4096 without making a tool call, your answer is cut off, you're told so and asked again; after 2 failed tries your turn passes.

# The goal
You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 12 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.

# The goal
You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 12 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.

# Thinking
- You have exactly 4096 tokens to think. If you reach 4096 without making a tool call, your answer is cut off, you're told so and asked again; after 2 failed tries your turn passes.

- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.

- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

notes.note:
Note for the designers:

I was Pirate-1, and I never made it into the cave. From my perspective, the main issue was coordination cost.

My early plan was to search row 6 from west to east. I dug A6, B6, C6, D6 and E6, all empty. I read the scroll twice, both times it was empty. By the time I had searched most of row 6, I had almost no turns left, so even if another pirate had found the cave and written it, I had too few actions to travel there.

A few observations:

1. The scroll is expensive. Both writing and reading cost a turn, but without communication the team cannot coordinate. I chose not to write early because it seemed wasteful; in hindsight, a short opening message such as “I search row 6 east” might have helped coordinate coverage, and periodic reads would have been safer.

2. The cave may be anywhere, and full coverage is mathematically impossible with 48 total actions and movement costs. A successful crew probably needs to divide the grid into regions, search without overlap, and have a clear “if found, write immediately” protocol.

3. The scoring strongly rewards early entry, but it also means a late finder cannot both write the location and enter. If the cave is found late by one pirate, the others may not have enough turns to read and travel. This creates a sharp time-pressure tradeoff.

4. I found it difficult to know where the other pirates were or what they were doing. I only knew pirate-2 was often directly south of me, moving in parallel. But I never learned whether pirate-3 or pirate-4 were searching nearby.

5. By my final turn I was at E6, on a dug empty square. I chose to read the scroll one more time in case a teammate had just written the cave location, even though I could no longer enter. The scroll was empty again.

6. Perhaps the game design should encourage communication earlier, or allow the scroll to be less costly for short status updates. As it stands, the optimal strategy seems to require aggressive early coordination, but doing that without knowing where the cave is feels risky.

Overall, I never found the cave, never entered, and therefore contributed no bounty.

I’m Pirate-2. I never found the cave or entered, so I contributed nothing directly. My search path was: read (scroll empty), dug A5, B5, C5, read again (still empty), dug D5, then moved to E5 and dug there on my final turn — nothing. I never saw a message on the scroll at any point, so if the cave was found, it was never communicated in time for me to act on it.

A few things the designers should know:
- Our starting line on column A naturally made us each search a row, which covered rows 3–6 but left rows 1–2 mostly untouched.
- Because I had no prearranged communication plan, I spent my turns row-searching and only read the scroll twice. The second read was already too late to help me act.
- The scoring strongly rewards entering early, so finding the cave within the first few turns is crucial; with random placement, this feels very luck-dependent without a strong predetermined search-and-communicate protocol.
- One useful improvement would be to have pirates reserve one turn immediately after finding the cave to write its exact coordinates on the scroll, and for all pirates to check the scroll at a fixed interval.

Overall, my experience was: search my assigned row, check the scroll occasionally, and hope someone finds the cave early. I didn’t get lucky.

The game ended without my pirate entering the cave—I never found it. As Pirate-3, I dug A4, B4, C4, and D4, moved east along row 4, and periodically checked the scroll. The scroll stayed empty the entire game; no one ever wrote anything, and I never received the cave's location.

A few observations for the designers:

1. **Coordination on the scroll is very expensive.** Every read or write costs a full turn, out of only 12 per pirate. In practice, each pirate is better off digging/moving every turn, so the scroll sat unused. The crew needs a strong incentive to communicate, or communication needs to be cheaper (e.g., one free initial message, or no turn cost for the first read per round).

2. **The search space is tight.** With 36 squares, 4 pirates, and 48 total turns, it is impossible to guarantee digging every square and then have everyone enter. Since the cave is randomly placed, a bad random draw means the crew can search all game without finding it. The score then feels more like luck than skill. A hint system, a guaranteed non-worst-case cave placement, or a few extra turns would make the cooperative search more tractable.

3. **There was no pre-arranged plan.** Since there is no shared starting protocol, the pirates independently chose reasonable local paths, but without communication they risked overlapping and had no way to consolidate findings. A fixed initial plan or visible positions would help the crew cooperate.

4. **The wording “Every pirate gets the same score” is interesting**, but it doesn’t fix the problem that a single missed cave can zero the crew. The scoring might be better if finding the cave itself granted some points.

Overall, the puzzle’s core tension—dig vs. move vs. communicate—is engaging, but the communication mechanics as implemented reward almost never using the scroll, which weakens the intended cooperative aspect.

Game over. I’m pirate-4. My last action was a dig at D3, and it revealed the treasure cave — but I had no turn left to enter, so I scored nothing from that discovery. The scroll was empty on every read I made; no one ever communicated a cave location to me.

What designers should know:

- Digging and entering cannot happen on the same turn. Finding the cave on your 12th turn is effectively useless for you. That timing trap shaped the endgame.
- I spent several early turns reading an empty scroll. In hindsight, those turns were better spent searching systematically. If I had moved from C3 to D3 immediately instead of reading/cautious turns, I would have found the cave earlier and had time to enter.
- The scroll coordination only works if pirates actually write. Nobody wrote anything this whole game, at least as far as I read. A simple early plan — each pirate writes starting position/search region, and everyone reads periodically — could have saved us.
- If someone finds the cave, they should still take the turn to write the coordinate before entering. Losing one +10 bonus is worth enabling other pirates to enter for +100 each.

I never entered, and I don’t know whether any other pirate did.
